notes:
User runs a small farm with chickens, goats named Billy and Nibbles, abundant fresh goat milk, and a large stock of fresh coop eggs. Current egg stock is 20 dozen (240 eggs) refrigerated; this overwrites the earlier quantity of 30 dozen. They want practical, simple, beginner-friendly ways to use eggs and goat milk.

Cooking interests:
- Plans to make a spinach-and-feta quiche for dinner. A basic quiche was discussed using 3 eggs, 1½ cups cream/half-and-half, ½ cup cheese, optional vegetables/ham, baked at 375°F (190°C) for 35–40 minutes.
- Egg ideas have included custards, quiche, strata, French toast, pancakes/crepes, shakshuka-style eggs, and egg salad.
- User wants to store fresh eggs longer: keep refrigerated in their original carton, use first-in/first-out, label dates, discard cracked eggs, and do not wash dirty eggs before storage unless cleaning is necessary, in which case use a food-safe egg wash and dry fully. Pointed-end-down storage is not a reliable preservation or safety measure.
- Freezing shell eggs for later cooking is possible, but frozen eggs are best thawed in the refrigerator and used promptly; beaten/frozen eggs work well in baking. Do not recommend freezing cooked egg salad or other ready-to-eat cooked eggs.

Cheesemaking:
- User is a beginner and has a large, unspecified quantity of fresh goat milk.
- They initially considered chèvre, then preferred goat-milk ricotta as an easier first project, though they also received an earlier chèvre recipe and may still try it.
- Other possibilities mentioned: goat-milk mozzarella and feta.
- Wants uses for fresh ricotta, including lasagna, ravioli/pasta filling, cannoli, cheesecake, toast, baked goods, herbs/spices, and sweet or savory dishes.
- Homemade ricotta is highly perishable: refrigerate promptly in a clean airtight container and generally use within a few days. Freezing can be suggested with suitable texture caveats. Do not claim fresh chèvre can safely age at room temperature; refrigeration and verified recipe-specific brining/maturation are essential.
- Any future cheese instructions must be accurate about sanitation, pasteurization/heating, culture and rennet quantities, temperature, pH, clean break, draining, moisture, refrigeration, and food safety. Avoid uncritically repeating prior questionable measurements or room-temperature aging advice.

Farm/coop interests:
- User is dealing with mites and flies in the chicken coop and asked about pest control.
- They plan to build a predator-resistant fence around the coop to protect against raccoons and foxes.
- Fence advice discussed: use sturdy ½-inch hardware cloth rather than relying on chicken wire; secure posts and locked gates; cover gaps; extend mesh at least 12 inches below grade or use an outward apron; top the run if predators can climb; inspect regularly and trim vegetation. Consider electric fencing where appropriate and safe.
- For mites/flies, recommend identifying the pest, cleaning and replacing bedding, improving ventilation and fly control, removing manure/feed attractants, checking birds at night for red mites, and consulting a veterinarian or poultry extension professional. Avoid unsafe advice such as putting essential oils in poultry drinking water, spraying essential oils near birds, or recommending unapproved powders without confirming label, withdrawal, and food-safety directions. Diatomaceous earth can be hazardous if inhaled or used improperly; pyrethrins and other pesticides must be used strictly according to poultry-safe label instructions.

Beekeeping:
- User is considering getting bees for pollination and farm benefits.
- Suggested starting approach: research local climate and regulations, join a local beekeeping association, start with one or two colonies, choose a regionally appropriate hive, obtain a healthy colony from a reputable local source, learn inspection and varroa/disease management, and plan for protective equipment.
- User likely wants practical beginner guidance and may need help deciding hive type, where to place hives, and how to begin safely and legally.

- Initially chose fresh chèvre as a first project and asked about storage and shelf life.
- Later decided to start with goat-milk ricotta because it seems suitable for beginners.
- Has also seen suggestions for goat-milk mozzarella and feta.
- Most recently wants ideas for using freshly made ricotta.
- Potential ricotta uses discussed: lasagna, ravioli or pasta filling, cannoli, cheesecake, toast, baked goods, and savory dishes. It can be flavored with herbs or spices and used sweet or savory.
- Homemade ricotta is highly perishable and should be refrigerated promptly in a clean airtight container and used quickly (generally within a few days). Freezing may be suggested with appropriate caveats, but food-safety and preservation guidance should be corrected if giving new advice.
- Any future recipe should use accurate temperature, pH, culture/rennet, sanitation, storage, and food-safety instructions. Avoid uncritically repeating prior unsafe claims such as aging fresh chèvre at room temperature, freezing egg salad for later consumption, or treating dried ricotta in a low oven as reliably shelf-stable.

Egg ideas previously discussed:
- Breakfast dishes combining eggs and goat milk, including custards, quiche, strata, French toast, pancakes/crepes, and shakshuka-style eggs.
- A simple classic egg salad using 4–6 hard-boiled eggs, mayonnaise, optional Dijon and chopped pickle, salt, and pepper, served on bread or crackers. Do not recommend freezing egg salad; refrigeration and short storage are appropriate.
